component.name: Refrain
component.summary: Fast, low-memory client for YouTube Music

description.p: Refrain is a desktop client for YouTube Music, written in Rust. It browses anonymously, or signs in using the browser cookies you already have — no separate login and no web view.
Features:

ul.li: Search organised into songs, videos, albums, artists and playlists
Home and library feeds, plus album, playlist and artist pages
Streaming playback with a disk cache, so replays start instantly
Thumbs up and down, shuffle, repeat and an "Up next" queue
Desktop media controls: media keys, the panel widget and playerctl
Light and dark themes, and keyboard shortcuts

screenshot.caption: An album playing, with the queue open

description.p: The queue can be edited: play next, add to queue, move an entry up or down, and remove one. It used to be a list you could look at and click, and nothing else.

Starting up no longer re-extracts browser cookies when there is no YouTube session to find. That extraction drives yt-dlp to fetch a video just to dump the cookies, and it was being paid on every launch before the first frame — measured at 12 seconds here, and 0.6 now.

Playback dropouts are reported rather than handled in silence: the buffer underruns the output device reports, and the reads that had to wait for the downloader. The two mean different things — the waits say the download is behind real time, the underruns alone point below it — and Settings shows both.
--underrun-test <id> [seconds] plays a track aloud and prints the same numbers, so a stutter can be settled on a machine with real audio.
An AppImage install now fetches the AppImage. It used to fetch the tarball and put it in the AppImage's place, which left a file that could not be executed.
A download whose contents do not match the kind of installation is refused before anything is replaced, and restarting no longer freezes the window while it watches the new build start.
Scrolling the feed has momentum: a flick glides to rest instead of stopping the instant the wheel does.
Streaming playback buffers to disk rather than to memory: a track that plays for four minutes no longer sits in RAM while it does, which is about 8 MB while something is playing.
Updates download to disk instead of into memory: a 52 MB release used to peak at 125 MB, and now peaks at 19.
Artwork is decoded at the size it is drawn rather than always at the largest, which cuts the memory a row of cover art costs by six.
The playing row's equaliser animates at the frame rate the platform delivers rather than at the four frames a second the rest of the player bar needs.
--fps reports that rate, for when an animation looks wrong and it matters whether the app or the display is to blame.
When a queue or an album ends, playback continues with related tracks from the track's radio, the way YouTube Music does. A setting turns it off.

Restarting after an update starts the new build without the environment the old one was running in, which could stop it coming up — and if it fails, the reason is now shown rather than left in a corner.
Lyrics for the track that is playing, in a tab beside the queue. Plain text: the responses YouTube serves carry no timing, so there is nothing to follow along with.
The category selector is its own control beside the search field again, rather than a chip inside it.

Settings checks for a newer release and installs it in place where that is safe: an AppImage, or a tarball unpacked by hand. A copy owned by a package manager is left alone. Downloads are checked against the published checksum before anything is replaced.

Playback keeps the queue when the audio device is rebuilt. It used to resume the current track but forget everything after it, so playback stopped for good when that track ended — after a suspend, a headset switch, or the sound server restarting.
The volume is saved when you change it. It used to be written only when something else happened to save the config, so a volume set in one session was often gone in the next.
The window carries its icon on Windows and macOS, and the desktop entry now matches the window on Linux, so docks and taskbars show the app rather than a placeholder.
The search field and the category picker are one control now, so they can no longer overlap, and the toolbar no longer shifts as a page loads.
Settings is grouped into sections, with the JavaScript runtime reported alongside yt-dlp and a meter for the audio cache.
Corrects the application ID in the AppStream metadata: a component that begins with a digit needs a leading underscore, and without one the ID is not a valid Flatpak application name.
The scripted demo no longer stalls waiting for a repaint.
Downloads carry QuickJS, so playback no longer needs a JavaScript runtime installed.
A cookies file can be picked in the app, which is how signing in works where reading a browser's store is not possible.
Packaged as an AppImage as well as a tarball.
Artwork is fetched only for what is on screen, and sign-in can be configured in the app rather than in the config file.
First release.
